chapter_theme: The king, out hunting, turns his killing on the ascetic Sudatta, looses hounds that will not come near him and draws his sword; the merchant Kalyanamitran stops him with the greatness of the ascetic, a former king of Kalinga, and with the rule that lives, even one's own, are not to be taken; the king bows and begs to hear of births, and Sudatta begins by his avadhi knowledge.

cast.role: the hunting king; unnamed in these verses
the ascetic Sudatta, a former king of Kalinga
the merchant who stops the king
Asokan, whose heaven the ascetic names; perhaps the king of Ujjayini of chapter 5

262.reading: With nets, snares and a hundred other hunting devices, and packs of tusk-toothed hounds baying, the king takes up his spear and speeds to the hunt in the midst of his four-fold army, like Death himself in the middle of a sea.
262.nuance: The simile makes the king Death (நமன்) before he has met the ascetic of the next verses; the poet loads the hunt with the image of killing.
262.event: The king sets out at speed on a hunt with his army, hounds and nets.

263.reading: The ascetic Sudatta, whose nature is to give living beings good, and who wipes away the dust of the two clinging kinds of deed, stands in his vow-posture; the king, proud and raging like a rutting elephant, thrusts in on him.
263.nuance: Line 2 reads தொத்திருவிளைத்துகள்; the sense is தொத்து இருவினைத் துகள் (clinging dust of the two deeds), so விளை stands for வினை. The last line, with இழித்து and அடுசுடத்திடை, is hard: whether the king dismounts, reviles, or sets something on the ascetic cannot be fixed, so the reading keeps to 'confronts'.
263.event: The raging king confronts the standing ascetic Sudatta.

claims.claim: the ascetic wipes away the dust of the two kinds of deed (good and bad) that cling to the soul

264.reading: Like Death combing the forest's edge, he has found nothing to kill that fits today, and so, saying he will end his whole business and take the sweet life of the one before him, he comes with unstoppable rage upon the great ascetic.
264.nuance: வினை முற்றும் பாற்றி may mean 'ending his whole day's labour' (the hunt) or, as a pun, 'wiping out [his] deeds'; the verse is ironical either way, since the ascetic is the one who wipes deeds away (263).
264.event: Finding no game, the king turns his killing intent on the ascetic.

265.reading: He looses at the lord, from whom a rain of grace pours, a pack of fire-breathing, barking hounds, as many as fifty doubled with five, as though they were going to seize red flesh.
265.nuance: The count (ஐந்தினொடு பொருத தொகை ஐம்பதின் இரட்டி) is read as about a hundred and five; the wording is loose. The contrast is the poem's: the one who rains grace is met with hounds sent for flesh.
265.event: The king sets his pack of hounds on the ascetic.

266.reading: By the power of the penance that does great dharma the hounds fear to touch him and stand off at a bow's distance; the king, black-hearted and swollen with rage, then thinks of loosing the cruel weapon himself and draws his sword.
266.nuance: The grammar of lines 2 and 3 is broken. The reading rests on 279, where the merchant says the hounds do not come near, and so on the hounds standing off; it is not certain that the verse says the hounds are what stand.
266.event: The hounds are held back by the ascetic's penance, and the king draws his sword.

267.reading: A strong merchant named Kalyanamitran, dear as the king's own life, comes between and cries that he is undone, for a sword is being drawn before the great ascetic.
267.nuance: எனை (line 4) can read as 'me': that the blade is drawn on him as he steps between, or that the king's sword, drawn at the ascetic, ruins the merchant too. Kalyanamitran is named only here in the chapter and the verse calls him a kinsman of the king, not his minister.
267.event: The merchant Kalyanamitran enters and protests the drawn sword.

268.reading: Cast off this rage, he says; instead of honouring the feet of one who bears the mountain-load of great dharma, why does a mind burning with anger take up a cruel weapon, O king of the garland and the fierce spear?

claims.claim: one who bears the great burden of dharma is to be honoured, and not attacked

269.reading: If they say 'let it be', it is; if they say 'let them be destroyed', they are; if they say 'let the cloud come here', it comes, and that too by fate: such is the greatness of the one-minded ascetics, O lord with the cloud-generous hand and the elephant-like heart.
269.nuance: விதியின் (line 2) makes the ascetic's power run through fate (விதி); it is not clear whether the ascetic's will is itself fate or whether fate is what lets the will take effect. The verse does not say the ascetic works by a god.

claims.claim: the will of one-minded ascetics is fulfilled, even to bringing the rain-cloud

270.reading: Those who come to them with love become lords of the gods, those who pass beyond them in contempt fall to the lowest hell; the venerable ones are like shade that one takes refuge in, with neither favour nor anger, and the course of the world beyond is the doing of the divine ones.
270.nuance: The fruit of honour and scorn falls on the doer, yet the ascetics themselves are said to hold neither favour nor wrath (அருளும் முனிவும் இலர்); the verse does not say who dispenses the result.

claims.claim: those who honour ascetics become lords of the gods and those who scorn them fall to the lowest hell
the holy ones are without favour or anger, like shade that shelters whoever comes

271.reading: Even if Indras come to bow at their feet, or others inflict endless bitter pain, they do not think 'ours' or 'others', only 'each one's own deed', these ascetic kings who have risen far above the world, O wearer of the garland.

claims.claim: suffering inflicted by another is the sufferer's own deed come back, and the ascetic sees no 'ours' or 'others'

272.reading: Every life in the world is like my own life, they hold; so, putting away cruelty and pouring grace, they raise up lives; bow at the holy feet of those who stand guard like the eyelid, and you will cross beyond your deeds, O victorious spear-bearer.
272.nuance: இமையின் in line 3 is read as 'like the eyelid' (which guards the eye); the text spells it விமையின், a possible misprint.

claims.claim: every life is equal to one's own life
bowing at the feet of the ascetics who guard lives carries one beyond one's deeds

273.reading: The king, not rejecting the merchant's gentle words, lays down his anger and the weapon in his hand, then asks who this pitiable man is that he, the king, should bow to, a dark-skinned man thick with dust.
273.nuance: He yields to the plea, not to the ascetic: the weapon goes down while contempt remains, so his turn to reverence is not yet made (283).
273.event: The king puts aside his anger and weapon but still scorns the dust-grimed ascetic.

claims.claim: a man grimed with dust is not worth the king's bowing

274.reading: If you ask whom the world worships, hear: he is the ornament of the Ganga line, lord of Kalinga, who ruled the whole land alone like a lion with no shared strength of arm; know this clearly, king.
274.nuance: The ascetic is not named in these lines; that he is Sudatta (263) is from the context. கங்கைகுல திலகன் is the Ganga dynasty of Kalinga, a claim about a person the verse does not date.
274.event: The merchant tells the king that the ascetic was once a king of Kalinga.

275.reading: Thinking that pleasure, wealth and youth pass quickly like cloud, lightning and the rainbow, he resolves on renunciation, the dharma in which grace grows, and sets his mind on entering the pleasure-rich golden world.
275.nuance: Line 3 is damaged (ஆகதுற வருள்பெருகு மறெனெடத னியலே). The aim named in line 4 is the heaven of pleasures, not release; compare 284, where the fruit is a divine world.
275.event: The king of Kalinga reasons that enjoyment is fleeting and resolves to renounce.

claims.claim: pleasure, wealth and youth are as fleeting as cloud, lightning and the rainbow

276.reading: Lands and cities, the women of fair loveliness, banner-waving elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers, crown, garland, earrings, shoulder-bangles, necklace and clothes: 'let all go away from me', he said, and gave them up.
276.event: Sudatta gives up kingdom, women, army, ornaments and clothes.

277.reading: Gods, kings of the earth and the mountain dwellers come to worship him as he takes the ascetic form, and with no taint in his mind, thinking only of what is good for lives, he wanders through forest, hills and lands.
277.nuance: Gods and kings worship him now, as the merchant said at 270 of those who come near.
277.event: Sudatta takes the ascetic form and wanders the forests while gods and kings worship him.

278.reading: Holding that 'I' is nothing, 'mine' is nothing and even benefit is nothing, the dignified ascetic delights not in his body; the dirt of other deeds does not stay in his form, and each day he wears the virtues that smile with the light of knowledge.
278.nuance: இதம் (benefit) is added to the pair 'I' and 'mine': he gives up even the good he might claim for himself, which goes past the Kural's pair.

claims.claim: the ascetic holds that neither 'I' nor 'mine' nor even benefit is real

279.reading: This is the greatness of the matchless ascetic's yoga, lord: the killing deed of the forest and the fierce karma that were to join you have ceased to join you today; why seek killing, spear-bearer? See, the hounds do not come near.
279.nuance: The deed is said to have stopped through the ascetic's greatness, which reads the stopping of karma as brought about by the ascetic's yoga; the verse does not say how.

claims.claim: the killing deed that was about to bind the king has been stopped before it joined him

280.reading: When the merchant has said this, to move his mind, the king goes, sets the holy lotus feet on his head, and thinks: 'to dissolve my fault today I will cut off my head and stand in refuge at his feet.'
280.nuance: The king's own measure of the fault is a life; the merchant answers it in 281 and 282.
280.event: The king resolves to cut off his own head as atonement.

claims.claim: a fault against an ascetic is wiped out by giving one's head at his feet

281.reading: Seeing him think this, the merchant raises his hand and says: let go what is in your mind, king; if one raises others' lives as one's own life, that is right; if you take your own life, what grace is that?
281.nuance: The same word for life, உயிர், covers both: the verse extends the rule that protects others' lives to the king's own.
281.event: The merchant stops the king from cutting off his own head.

claims.claim: it is right to nourish others' lives like one's own, and destroying one's own life is not grace

282.reading: The matter he spoke before is not finished; more remains to be said, and the sense of what he thinks to say now comes to him: having decided this earlier, do not fill up the fault; what you now think of is a great harm, he said.
282.nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are very hard; பிழைதூராய் may mean 'do not heap fault' or 'do not leave the fault undone'. Only the last line, that the new plan is a great harm, is certain.

283.reading: Giving up the king's rage and growing in grace, he goes to the feet of Sudatta, whose speech is full of eloquence, bows so that the flowers of his crown touch them, and speaks of all of their births.
283.nuance: The last line is cut short: எமர் பவமுழுதும் is read as asking to hear the whole of their births, which the muni's knowledge in 284 can supply. He has gone from the weapon of 266 to the crown-flowers on the feet, and it is the merchant, not the ascetic, who brought this about.
283.event: The king bows at Sudatta's feet and asks him of their births.

284.reading: Then the ascetic, setting out by his avadhi knowledge what it had shown him so that the king could take it in, tells that Asokan, by the penance he did before, rejoiced in a divine world of high fame.
284.nuance: Whether this Asokan is Yasodharan's father of ch. 5 is not stated in the verse; same name is not shown to be same person. அவதி is the clairvoyant knowledge of the Jain ascetic, here used for knowledge of former births.
284.event: Sudatta begins to reveal by his avadhi knowledge that Asokan reached a heaven through earlier penance.

claims.claim: the ascetic's earlier penance brings rebirth in a divine world

links.note: The hounds loosed in 265 to seize flesh are shown in 279 not coming near the ascetic.
links.teaches: The weapon that the king relied on is turned back by the very one it was loosed on, so the story shows his force failing before his remorse begins.

links.note: In 67 and here a king puts down the weapon in his hand under pressure of a speech; in 67 it is the victim's own sermon, here a third party's plea.
links.teaches: The two scenes show that the sword is laid down for different reasons: there the king is moved by what the victim teaches, here by what a friend says of the victim's greatness.

links.note: In 273 the king puts down the weapon but scorns the dust-grimed man; in 283 he bows so that his crown-flowers touch the ascetic's feet.
links.teaches: The king's change is made in two steps, so the first (weapon) does not yet carry the second (reverence).

links.note: 274 says he ruled the whole land alone like a lion; 276 has him cast off that land, women and army.
links.teaches: What the king of Kalinga gives up in 276 is given its size by the merchant's earlier account of how entirely he held it.

links.note: In 82 Asokan reasons that greater merit now may win Indra's world; in 284 the ascetic says Asokan reached a divine world by earlier penance.
links.teaches: Asokan's reasoning about merit is shown to bring about the heaven he had thought of, only now told by another.

links.note: 81 says youth and kinship are fleeting and the mind should leave them; 275 adds wealth and pleasure and ends with the pleasure-rich heaven as the aim.
links.teaches: The same impermanence argument that leads one king to give up the kingdom is shown aiming at heaven rather than release, in both.

links.note: 280 has the king resolve to offer his own head; 281 says that to destroy one's own life is not grace.
links.teaches: The rule against killing is used here to forbid an act of reverence by the doer on himself, and so it does not give way to atonement.

links.note: In 270 the fruit follows honour or scorn though the ascetics hold neither favour nor anger; in Tirumanthiram 36 grace comes in the measure of the praise.
links.teaches: One text lets the result come from the one who honours without any granting, the other makes the Lord answer; the two differ over whether anyone grants the fruit.

gains.a: The epic verse lacks any figure who gives the fruit, and the Saiva verse shows what the ascetic's indifference excludes: a giver.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse lacks the Jain case in which a reverence has result with no one pleased by it.

links.note: 271 says the ascetic thinks of pain inflicted as his own deed; Naladiyar 58 says the worthy grieve for those who scorn them, fearing the hell that will follow.
links.teaches: Together they show that holding hurt as one's own deed does not leave the ascetic cold: Naladiyar adds the pity for the offender that 271 omits.

gains.a: 271 gains a feeling for the offender that its karma explanation leaves out.
gains.b: Naladiyar 58 gains a king with dogs as its case: the scorner is shown at the moment before the fall it fears for him.

links.note: 272 grounds 'all lives are like my own' in an ascetic's grace and a result beyond karma; Kural 315 tests understanding by guarding another's pain as one's own.
links.teaches: The epic puts the rule into a speech to a hunting king, so that guarding other lives has a named cost to him: his hounds and spear.

gains.a: 272 gains the Kural's plain test: understanding that does not guard another's pain is empty.
gains.b: Kural 315 gains a person who does the opposite, a king hunting with a pack.

links.note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; 281 forbids the king to take his own life even to atone.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule against killing is shown to cover the doer's own life, which the couplet does not say.

gains.a: 281 gains a forceful general rule against taking life, with no exception for need.
gains.b: Kural 327 gains the opposite case, where the life endangered is one's own, to be spared in atonement.

links.note: 278 has the ascetic hold neither 'I' nor 'mine' nor even benefit; Kural 346 says cutting off 'I' and 'mine' reaches a world above the gods.
links.teaches: The epic adds a third term, benefit, to the Kural's pair, so letting go includes even what one might claim as one's own good.

gains.a: 278 gains the Kural's statement that this giving up has a result beyond the gods' world.
gains.b: Kural 346 gains a figure who has done it, a king turned ascetic.

links.note: Naladiyar 53 has the best renounce home, youth and wealth at once to save themselves; 275 renounces for the pleasure-rich heaven.
links.teaches: The epic shows that the same reflection on impermanence may end in heaven rather than in release.

gains.a: 275 gains Naladiyar's view that the point of renunciation is saving oneself.
gains.b: Naladiyar 53 gains an instance in which the reflection leads to a heaven of pleasure, not release.

links.note: Kural 28 says the greatness of those whose word is full shows in their hidden words; 269 says what such ascetics will comes about, even the cloud, and puts this under fate.
links.teaches: The epic places the ascetic's power in his will and under fate, where the couplet puts it in the word.

gains.a: 269 gains the Kural's claim that greatness is known through the word.
gains.b: Kural 28 gains a kind of proof, rain and destruction at the ascetic's will.

new_concepts.gloss: the Jain ascetic's limited clairvoyance, here knowledge of former births

source_issues: Verse 263 line 2 reads விளைத்துகள் where வினைத்துகள் is meant.
Verse 266 lines 2 and 3 do not parse; 275 line 3 is damaged; 282 lines 1 to 3 and 283 line 4 are hard to construe.
Verse 272 line 3 spells இமையின் as விமையின்.
